questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A supply chain that creates dependency
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a supply chain creates dependency and what a break would do
questions.stem: At the apiary I was explaining why one region's honey now travels a long way before it reaches a shop. Which statement best describes what has created that dependency?

options.text: The chain exists because every stage is owned by the same family, so no one can withdraw it
options.misconception: explains dependency as the result of common ownership

options.text: The chain exists because each stage is the cheapest option, so no firm would ever want to change it
options.misconception: treats lowest cost as a permanent guarantee of supply

options.text: The chain exists because laws force each stage to buy from the stage before it
options.misconception: confuses commercial reliance with legal compulsion

options.text: The chain exists because each stage depends on goods from the next, so stopping one link halts the others

questions.explanation: Dependency arises because each stage needs the output of the others, so a break anywhere stops the whole chain. Shared ownership, cheapness and legal compulsion describe other reasons.
questions.hint: Ask what happens if one link stops working.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A line that stops
questions.learningObjective: Analyse the effects of a break in one link of a supply chain

stimulus.body: Logbook entry for 14 May: the long line of hives that carried frames south by road has stopped. The truck that ran that route is off the road for repair, the railway siding that carried hives is closed for track work, and the ferry that took crates across the water is not running this season. My neighbour says the bees are fine; the honey is not moving.

questions.stem: Judging from the logbook entry above, what does the stopped line of supply illustrate?

options.text: A shortage of bees, since hives cannot be replaced quickly enough at the other end
options.misconception: confuses a broken supply route with a shortage of bees

options.text: A break in one link, where every other stage is ready but the route between them has failed
A fall in demand, since buyers have stopped ordering honey from the southern hives
options.misconception: assumes buyers abandoned the product rather than the route

options.text: A storage problem, since the honey cannot be kept at the apiary until buyers come
options.misconception: jumps to a storage explanation not mentioned in the entry

questions.explanation: The entry says the bees and buyers are unaffected while the road, rail and ferry routes are unavailable, which is a break in one link. Shortages of bees and lost demand are excluded.
questions.hint: Notice what the entry says is still working.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Who gains inside one country
questions.learningObjective: Identify who gains and loses inside one country from a change in import prices
questions.stem: In my hive log I noted which part of a country's economy gains when a raw material for beekeeping becomes dearer. Explain who benefits inside one country when the price of an imported input rises, and why.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would say that within the single country, producers of the domestic substitute for that imported input gain, because their goods now face less competition and can command a higher price. It would add that firms using the imported input as a raw material lose, since their costs rise and they must either absorb them or pass them on, and that the government may gain a little extra tax revenue while the country as a whole is worse off because the input now costs more.

questions.explanation: The item tests the domestic split between substitute producers and input users. Answers that name only one group, or that claim the whole country gains, miss who actually bears the cost.
questions.hint: Think about who makes the substitute and who uses the input.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Gains and losses in different places
questions.learningObjective: Compare gains and losses across countries from a tariff change
questions.stem: I asked a neighbour to compare a honey market before and after an import tariff was cut. Which statement describes the distributional effects across the two countries most accurately?

options.text: Both countries gain because cheaper honey is bought in larger quantities by everyone
options.misconception: ignores the losses suffered by the protected producers

options.text: The exporting country gains market share and the importing country's producers lose, while its buyers gain
The exporting country loses and the importing country gains, because trade always benefits both
options.misconception: reverses which side is helped by cheaper imports

options.text: Neither side changes, because a tariff cut only moves money between the two governments
options.misconception: claims tariff cuts alter no private market outcome

questions.explanation: Cutting the tariff lets the exporting country sell more, helping its producers and hurting the importing country's protected producers, while buyers gain. Costless-change answers miss the losses.
questions.hint: Ask who loses when the protected price falls.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A review of quotas and votes
questions.learningObjective: Describe how quotas and votes are allocated in a reviewed system

stimulus.body: Meeting note: the branch meeting reviewed how export quotas and the votes on them are shared out. The note recorded that quotas are allocated between producing districts in a fixed formula based on past output, and that the vote on any change is taken by simple majority of the delegates present. Several members said the formula was agreed many years ago and had never been redrawn.

questions.stem: The branch meeting reviewed how export quotas and votes are run and found what?

options.text: Quotas are set by each district for itself, and votes are taken to confirm the district's own choice
options.misconception: reads self-set quotas with confirmatory votes as shared

options.text: Quotas are negotiated anew each year, and each district holds an outright veto over any change
options.misconception: confuses a majority rule with a veto held by one district

options.text: Quotas are divided by historical output, and votes are weighted so that large districts carry the decision
options.misconception: assumes vote weighting where a simple majority is specified

options.text: Quotas are divided by a fixed historical formula, and votes on changes follow a simple majority rule

questions.explanation: The note states a fixed historical formula for quotas and a simple majority of delegates for votes, which the correct option reproduces. Self-set quotas, a veto and weighted voting are ruled out.
questions.hint: Quote the two rules the note actually records.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The quota rule behind the votes
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effects of a quota rule based on past output
questions.stem: While sealing jars I tried to explain why the votes on export quotas come out as they do. Which explanation best accounts for a rule that divides quotas by past output?

options.text: It is fair because every district gains an equal share regardless of what it produces
options.misconception: confuses proportional shares with equal shares

options.text: It is efficient because it guarantees the goods come from the districts with the lowest costs
options.misconception: assumes historic output reveals current cost advantage

options.text: It simplifies administration by removing any need to record actual production
options.misconception: claims the rule avoids record keeping it actually depends on

options.text: It rewards established producers and locks new districts out of the export market

questions.explanation: A rule based on past output entrenches the producers who already supplied, so districts without a record are shut out of the export market. Equal shares and cost leadership are different effects.
questions.hint: Ask who already has a record of production.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A programme attached to a loan
questions.learningObjective: Analyse a loan programme with attached purchase conditions
questions.stem: While the honey was settling I explained how money can be lent to a country on condition that it buys goods from the lender. Explain how such a programme works and why it can be criticised.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would say the lender provides a large loan and requires that a set share of the money be spent on goods from the lender's own exporters, with the loan repaid out of those receipts. It would add that critics call it a disguised export subsidy and a way of tying a commercial advantage to a financial decision, and that defenders reply the loan gives the borrowing country capital it could not raise on its own terms and holds down the risk for both sides.

questions.explanation: The item tests the mechanism of tying a loan to purchases and the standard criticism of it. Answers describing the loan without the condition, or that omit the criticism, miss the point.
questions.hint: Ask what the borrower must spend the money on.

questions.topic: Conditions written into an agreement
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of conditions written into an agreement

stimulus.body: Logbook entry for 2 July: I copied the terms of the old agreement into the hive book for reference. The money is released in stages as the borrower meets written conditions: opening the lines for inspection, keeping the agreed prices, and shipping a set quantity of the crop each season. If the conditions are broken the balance of the loan is held back rather than demanded at once.

questions.stem: The logbook entry above shows what effect from writing such conditions?

options.text: The agreement removes the need for any inspection of how the money was used
options.misconception: concludes the opposite of what the inspection clause implies

options.text: The borrower gains a guarantee that the full sum will always be released on schedule
options.misconception: reads conditional release as an unconditional promise to pay

options.text: Both sides gain a fixed price for the crop for the whole period of the loan
options.misconception: assumes a price guarantee the conditions do not create

options.text: The lender gains a way to check progress and to withhold the money if terms are broken

questions.explanation: Staged release with written conditions gives the lender oversight and a lever to withhold funds when terms are broken. The entry promises no unconditional payment and no fixed crop price.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the money when terms fail.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how reliance between stages creates dependency
questions.stem: A question at the apiary asked why a humble beekeeping chain could become the backbone of a whole country's economy. Which statement best describes that dependency?

options.misconception: assumes short chains insulate buyers from disruption

options.text: Because every stage is owned by the state, so no private firm can ever withdraw from it
options.misconception: explains dependency through ownership rather than reliance

options.text: Because the product is identical everywhere, so no buyer can choose a different supplier
options.misconception: claims no buyer could switch suppliers at all

options.text: Because every stage relies on the stage before it, so a break in one part stops the whole chain

questions.explanation: Dependency grows out of reliance: each stage needs the output of the one before, so a failure anywhere stops delivery. Shortness, state ownership and identical products would each weaken reliance.
questions.hint: Ask what each stage would do without the previous one.

stimulus.body: Logbook entry for 30 June: the railway that carried wax and frames to the press has been closed for track renewal, so no wax reaches the factory this month. options.text: A shortage of bees, since no wax is being produced to send to the factory
options.misconception: ignores the entry that the crop was produced as usual

options.text: A broken link in the chain, where production and demand are unaffected but transport is not
A fall in demand, since the shopkeepers have stopped ordering candles

options.text: An over-supply of frames, since the hives are producing more than the market needs
options.misconception: invents an oversupply that the entry never mentions

questions.explanation: The entry separates what is working from what is not: the crop is ready and buyers still order, while the route has stopped. That is a broken link, not a shortage of bees or lost demand.

options.misconception: reverses which group gains from dearer imports

options.text: The producers of the domestic substitute, because they face less competition in the home market
The government, because higher import prices always increase the tax collected at the border

The protected local producers gain, since lower prices always increase the market overall

options.misconception: invents a risk the market note never mentions

questions.explanation: The note shows buyers and foreign exporters benefiting while protected local jam makers and the beekeepers behind them lose. Options protecting the local makers ignore what the note records.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A review of quotas and votes
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the quota rule and the voting rule interact
questions.stem: Between two hive inspections I described how quotas and the votes on them are worked out. Explain how the two rules interact, and what the combination tends to produce.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would say that quotas are divided by a formula drawn from past output while changes to the arrangement are decided by a simple majority of delegates. Because the formula rewards districts with an established record, and because the majority rule gives no single district a veto, the combination tends to keep the big established districts in control of both the size of the shares and the pace of any change to the system.

questions.explanation: The item tests the link between how shares are calculated and how they are changed. Answers that describe either rule alone, or that assume the majority rule cancels the formula, miss the interaction.
questions.hint: Ask who benefits from a rule based on past output.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the effects of a quota rule based on past output
questions.stem: While the wax melted I tried to explain why a quota rule drawn up decades ago still shapes trade today. Which explanation best accounts for that persistence?

options.text: Because quotas are fixed by nature, so no government can alter the shares without physical change
options.misconception: treats administrative shares as though they were natural

options.text: Because the rule rewards the newest districts, giving them a reason to keep the system unchanged
options.misconception: reverses which districts the rule rewards

options.text: Because votes on the rule require unanimity, so no district can ever propose a change
options.misconception: assumes unanimity where a majority decides

options.text: Because the rule was drawn from past output, so it entrenches those already holding the largest shares

questions.explanation: A rule built on past output keeps the largest shares with the districts that already had them, and those districts have every reason to keep it. Rewards for newcomers are excluded.

stimulus.body: Reading note: the scheme I read about lends money to a country that cannot borrow cheaply on its own, and the loan must be spent on equipment and supplies bought from the lender. options.misconception: ignores the purchase condition described in the note

options.text: A loan tied to buying from the lender, criticised as a disguised subsidy to that lender's exporters
A grant of equipment, criticised for ignoring the country's own manufacturing base

options.text: A currency agreement, criticised for tying exchange rates to a foreign government's policy
options.misconception: mistakes a trade condition for an exchange rate commitment

questions.explanation: The note describes a loan conditional on buying from the lender, and the critic's charge that this favours the lender's exporters. The other options remove the condition or change the instrument.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A supply chain that creates dependency
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a supply chain creates dependency and what a break would do
questions.stem: I recorded in my log that a country has come to depend on a long chain for one product, and that officials fear any break. Explain what creates that dependency and what a break in the chain would do.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would say the dependency was built stage by stage, with each firm specialising in one narrow step and buying the neighbouring step from someone else, so that no single firm could work without the others. It would add that this arrangement is efficient in normal times because each stage can use specialised equipment and skilled labour, but that it is fragile: if one link cannot deliver, or cannot obtain the inputs to deliver, every stage after it stops as well, and the shock passes straight to the final price.

questions.explanation: The item tests both how the dependency arose and why it magnifies a single failure. Answers that describe specialisation without the knock-on effect, or that omit the efficiency, are incomplete.
questions.hint: Ask what a single missing link does to the rest.

stimulus.body: Logbook entry for 9 September: the road across the moor was closed by a landslide for eleven weeks. My husband says the chain did not stop; it merely shrank and lost money.

questions.stem: The landslide entry I copied records what happening to the supply line?

options.misconception: contradicts the entry that the packing shed stayed open

options.text: It continued at a smaller scale, with output sold locally at a lower price
It continued unchanged, since only the final wholesale step was affected by the closure
options.misconception: ignores the large drop in price the entry records

questions.explanation: The entry says production continued while the bulk route stayed shut, so output was sold locally at a lower price and the chain shrank rather than stopped. A full halt contradicts it.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would say the reliance grew because each step in the chain was set up to be efficient on its own, with the specialised supplier able to make the input better and cheaper than local firms, so buying it became cheaper than making it. options.misconception: assumes concentration is about geography, not reliance

options.text: A long chain has many steps, while a dependent chain has steps with no practical alternative available

questions.explanation: Dependence turns on whether a stage has a real alternative: a chain with no alternatives inherits every upstream failure, however many stages it has. Length alone tells little.
questions.hint: Ask whether any other supplier could step in.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A line that stops
questions.learningObjective: Analyse the effects of a break in one link of a supply chain

stimulus.body: Logbook entry for 7 June: the flour mill that supplies the bee-feed cakes has shut for repairs, so no feed has come for a fortnight. The bees are storing what they can, the shop has bread as usual, and the price of imported flour has not moved. I have written that the trouble is in one building in one town and has not yet reached the shelf.

questions.stem: The flour mill closure in my entry shows what about the chain?

options.text: That a shortage of bees has begun, since without feed the hives will not survive
options.misconception: ignores the entry that the bees are storing what they can

options.text: That the price of bread in the shop will fall, since flour is now available in excess
options.misconception: invents a surplus and a price fall the entry excludes

options.text: That a single upstream break has reached the chain without yet changing shop prices
That foreign flour producers are now taking all the market from the local mill
options.misconception: assumes a foreign takeover the entry does not record

questions.explanation: The entry records one upstream failure whose effect has not yet reached the shelf, with prices unchanged. A bee shortage and a foreign takeover are excluded by the entry's details.
questions.hint: Notice what has not changed yet.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Who gains inside one country
questions.learningObjective: Identify who gains and loses inside one country from a change in import prices
questions.stem: I set a puzzle for the young beekeeper about who benefits when a foreign product becomes more expensive. Which group inside the country actually gains?

options.text: The firms that use the imported product, because their material costs have risen so they can charge more
options.misconception: confuses a rise in input costs with a gain for the user

options.text: The home producers of the same product, because buyers can now get it more cheaply at home
The foreign exporters, because a higher price abroad always improves their margin
options.misconception: assumes a price rise abroad always benefits the seller

options.text: The households who buy the product, because they are now paying more for it
options.misconception: claims higher prices benefit the buyer

questions.explanation: Home producers of the competing good gain, because buyers switch to the cheaper domestic option once the import becomes dearer. Input users, foreign sellers and buyers of the import all lose.
questions.hint: Ask who now supplies the buyer instead.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Gains and losses in different places
questions.learningObjective: Compare gains and losses across countries from a tariff change

stimulus.body: Market note: the duty on imported wax was removed last autumn. The local wax press has increased output and taken on two extra workers, while the shop reports that more customers now buy candles made from local wax because they are cheaper than the imported ones. The importer's sales have fallen by a third, and the county records show less duty collected at the border.

questions.stem: The note on the wax duty supports which statement about the change?

options.text: Local producers and local buyers gain, while the importer and border revenue lose
Local producers and local buyers lose, since removing a duty always cuts home demand
options.misconception: contradicts the note that local sales of candles rose

options.text: Only the local producer gains, since the importer and the treasury are unaffected
options.misconception: ignores the falls the note records for both

options.text: Only the importer loses, since the county's producers and buyers see no change at all
options.misconception: denies the local gains the note describes

questions.explanation: The note records gains for the local wax press and for local buyers choosing cheaper candles, with lower importer sales and less border duty. Options reversing these movements are unsupported.
questions.hint: Read the note for what rose and what fell.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A review of quotas and votes
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the quota rule and the voting rule interact
questions.stem: My notes record a review of quotas and votes that ended with the rule changed for the first time in thirty years. Explain how that change became possible under the rules I described.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would say that the quota shares had been fixed by a formula drawn from deliveries in an old base year, which entrenched the districts that were producing then, and that changes were decided by a simple majority of delegates. Change became possible because the block of districts that had been locked out of the export market grew in number until, together with others, they could carry a majority and replace the base year with a current one, so the formula began to reward present output rather than past output.

questions.explanation: The item tests how the two rules can combine to produce reform. Answers that treat a change as a matter of goodwill, or that assume the formula alone fixed the outcome, miss the mechanism.
questions.hint: Ask when the newer districts gained their vote.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The quota rule behind the votes
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effects of a quota rule based on past output
questions.stem: Someone at the meeting proposed that the quota rule should be changed so that shares follow current output instead of past output. Which assessment of that proposal is most balanced?

options.text: It should be rejected, because any rule tied to output rewards firms that pollute the hives
options.misconception: invents an environmental objection the case never raises

options.text: It should be adopted at once, because no rule based on past output has ever worked anywhere
options.misconception: supports the proposal with a sweeping unsupported claim

options.text: It would reward current performance but would take shares from districts that built the export trade
It changes nothing in practice, because the voting rule already adjusts shares by itself
options.misconception: claims the voting rule performs the formula's work

questions.explanation: Moving to current output would favour districts producing now, but it would cut the shares of older districts that built the trade under the old rule. Other objections are invented.
questions.hint: Ask who gains and who gives up shares.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A programme attached to a loan
questions.learningObjective: Analyse a loan programme with attached purchase conditions

stimulus.body: Reading note: the article described a scheme under which a government borrows from abroad and the lender insists that a fixed share of the money goes to buying goods from the lender's own country. The article noted that the borrower obtains finance it could not raise cheaply on its own, and that the lender's manufacturers receive a guaranteed market. It also noted that critics call the arrangement a disguised subsidy for those manufacturers.

questions.stem: The article about the tied loan fits which statement best?

options.text: The scheme is an unconditioned gift of money, and the critics are said to be mistaken
options.misconception: ignores the purchase condition the note describes

options.text: The scheme ties a loan to purchases from the lender and is criticised as a hidden subsidy
The scheme is a currency agreement that fixes the borrower's exchange rate
options.misconception: mistakes a purchase condition for a currency commitment

options.text: The scheme reduces the lender's access to the borrower's market for its own goods
options.misconception: reverses which side gains a captive market

questions.explanation: The note describes a loan conditioned on buying from the lender, with the borrower's gain, the lender's guaranteed market and the standard criticism. A gift and a currency deal are excluded.
questions.hint: Ask what the lender's manufacturers get.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Conditions written into an agreement
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of conditions written into an agreement
questions.stem: While the smoker cooled I explained to a beginner why lenders and buyers write conditions into agreements. Which statement is correct?

options.text: They create agreed points to inspect and a remedy to apply when a term is not met
They remove every risk for both sides, so no dispute can ever arise later on
options.misconception: claims written terms can remove all risk

options.text: They set the price of every future delivery of the goods covered by the agreement
options.misconception: assumes conditions fix prices, which they do not

options.text: They let whichever party is stronger decide the terms without any agreement at all
options.misconception: describes imposition rather than a written agreement

questions.explanation: Written conditions give the parties agreed points to inspect and a remedy when a term fails, which is why they are written down. Removing all risk and fixing prices are different things.
questions.hint: Ask what the conditions let the parties check.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A supply chain that creates dependency
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a supply chain creates dependency and what a break would do
questions.stem: Planners in the county asked me why the honey trade now runs through three firms they cannot do without. Explain what makes this dangerous and what a planner should do about it.

answer.exemplar: A model answer would say the danger lies in concentration: with three essential suppliers and no developed alternatives, a single failure, strike, transport closure or policy change anywhere along the line stops production that has already been paid for, and there is no way to substitute the missing part in the short run. It would add that a planner should map the chain, identify the single points of failure, build or sponsor alternative suppliers, hold stocks of the parts most likely to be interrupted, and keep enough of its own spare capacity to cover the worst case for a season.

questions.explanation: The item tests both the diagnosis of concentrated dependence and the practical response. Answers naming the risk without a remedy, or a remedy without the risk, are incomplete.
questions.hint: Ask what a planner could actually change.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A line that stops
questions.learningObjective: Analyse the effects of a break in one link of a supply chain

stimulus.body: Logbook entry for 25 August: the lorry that took jars to the wholesale market was written off, so we could not send anything this week. We made the honey into bars instead and sold them at the farm gate for less than the wholesale price, and the shop in the village bought every bar. The record shows the season's tonnage down by a fifth, the money received down by more, and the bees entirely unaffected.

questions.stem: The entry about the written-off lorry records what happening after the failure?

options.text: The whole harvest was lost, because honey cannot be sold without the lorry
options.misconception: ignores the farm gate and village sales

options.text: Nothing changed, because the harvest was sold as usual at the same price
options.misconception: contradicts the fall in tonnage and in money received

options.text: The chain shortened and sold at lower prices and smaller volumes, without losing the harvest
The harvest was destroyed, since unsold honey cannot be kept at all
options.misconception: claims spoilage that the entry never describes

questions.explanation: The entry records a rerouted and shortened chain: less tonnage sold, less money taken, and nothing lost, with the bees unaffected. Total loss and destruction contradict the entry.
questions.hint: Compare the tonnage and the money in the record.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Who gains inside one country
questions.learningObjective: Identify who gains and loses inside one country from a change in import prices
questions.stem: The question of dearer and cheaper imports was put to me, and I was asked to handle both cases at once. Which statement does so correctly?

options.text: A dearer import helps home producers and hurts the government, while a cheaper one reverses both effects
options.misconception: leaves the effects on buyers and input users unstated

options.text: A dearer import helps home substitutes and hurts firms using it, while a cheaper import reverses this
A dearer import helps everyone because home makers can charge more for their goods
options.misconception: claims a benefit for buyers that does not exist

options.text: A cheaper import helps home producers, since buyers who switch bring more demand home
options.misconception: reverses which producers gain in the cheaper case

questions.explanation: When an import becomes dearer, home substitutes gain and input users lose; when it becomes cheaper, those positions swap. The other statements omit buyers and users or reverse who gains.
questions.hint: Track who switches, and in which direction.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Gains and losses in different places
questions.learningObjective: Compare gains and losses across countries from a tariff change

stimulus.body: Market note: the duty on imported honey was cut at the start of the year. The shop reports that jars are now noticeably cheaper and that customers buy more of them, though a lot of those customers switched from local honey rather than increasing the total they eat. Two local producers have cut their prices and one has closed. The cooperative across the border says its shipments are up by half.

questions.stem: The last market note in the book describes the effects of the cut how?

options.text: Buyers and the foreign cooperative gain, while some local producers lose sales and margin
Local producers gain, since customers who switched now buy their jars more often
options.misconception: ignores that the switch came out of local honey sales

options.text: Nothing changes overall, because customers only switched between products they already bought
options.misconception: treats switching between products as no change at all

options.text: Only the foreign cooperative gains, since prices at the shop are set by its exporters
options.misconception: claims the shop price is set abroad

questions.explanation: The note shows buyers paying less and buying more, the foreign cooperative shipping half as much again, and local producers cutting prices with one closing. The other statements contradict that.
questions.hint: Ask who switched away from local honey.
